points: 1 Problem: a technical correspondence rebutting Gan & Tao (SIGMOD 2015). It accepts their Ω(n^4/3) lower bound for Euclidean DBSCAN in d ≥ 3. It disputes four statements: the '17-year mis-claim' framing, 'intractable in practice', the restriction to Euclidean distance, and the experimental support for 'should replace DBSCAN on big data'.

2 Concession: the KDD'96 O(n log n) runtime was an informal average-case statement. It rested on a wrong O(log n) assumption for 'small' R*-tree range queries and was never a worst-case claim. The O(n²) worst case was already known, e.g. from GDBSCAN/Sander et al.

3 Algorithm and cost: exactly one RangeQuery per point, giving runtime O(C + n·Q + Σ r_i). A linear scan gives Θ(n²·D), and expensive distances such as SNN can reach O(n³). DBSCAN works with any distance and data type.

4 Theory (Theorems 3.1/3.2): USEC reduces to ε-range queries and BCP to nearest-neighbour queries. Under Hopcroft hardness, either a query costs Ω(n^1/3) or preprocessing costs Ω(n^4/3). So no universal index gives O(log n) queries with O(n log n) construction, yet Ω(n^4/3) still allows speedups over Θ(n²).

5 Grid critique: Gan & Tao's method touches O(1+(1/ρ)^{d−1}) boundary cells, with ρ = 1/1000 suggested. It works only for point data with Minkowski/Euclidean distance. Cutting ε from 5,000 to 1,000 in 7-D multiplies the theoretical grid cells by 5^7 = 78,125, which explains why their runtime falls as ε grows.

6 Parameter heuristics: minPts = 4 for 2-D data, or 2·dim. Choose ε as small as possible from a sorted k-distance plot (k = minPts − 1; k = 4, 13, 99 on Household). On Household this gives a cut between ε ≈ 500 and 2,000, with ε ≤ 1,000 typically better, whereas Gan & Tao use ε ≥ 5,000.

7 Red flags: noise should usually be 1%–30%. If the largest cluster holds more than 20%–50% of clustered points, use a smaller ε or OPTICS/HDBSCAN*. On Household at ε = 5,000, more than 99% of points sit in one cluster. The heuristics give ε < 500 (noise) and ε ≤ 400 (largest component), so the interesting range is ε = 100–500. Jumps at ε ≈ 500 and 3,500 are low-resolution artefacts.

8 Setup: Gan & Tao's three datasets (Household, Farm, PAMAP2) and their C++ binary, which includes the new method plus GriDBSCAN, R-tree and KDD'96 reimplementations. Compared against ELKI 0.7.0 Java (R*-tree, k-d tree, cover tree) and the authors' own C++ DBSCAN (ANN k-d tree, cover tree). Run on one Debian PC (i7-3770, 32 GB). Results are shown in plots only.

9 Main runtime result on Household: for ε < 500 every index gives a 10–1000× speedup over linear scan. Up to ε = 2,000 the new method is beaten by Gan & Tao's own GriDBSCAN and R-tree; it beats GriDBSCAN only for ε ≥ 3,000. The ANN k-d tree is usually fastest. At ε < 1,000 the largest cluster holds about 29% of the data and 84% of the data falls in 47 clusters.

10 Farm and PAMAP2: interesting ranges are ε ∈ [400; 1,000] (≈900) for Farm and [500; 2,000] for PAMAP2. At ε = 5,000 nearly everything merges; on PAMAP2 two clusters hold 99.6%. The authors suspect the timestamp was left in before PCA. Index-based, GriDBSCAN and KDD'96 implementations again beat the new method at smaller ε. Caveats: no cluster-utility evaluation, and the datasets may be the 'wrong' ones.

errors.quote: Sudden jumps near ε ≈ 500 and ε ≈ 3,500 are artifacts of low numerical resolution: attributes have as few as 32 distinct values, and 5% of records are duplicates (pp. 11–12).
errors.paper: p. 12 attributes the jumps only to low numerical resolution: with as few as 32 values per attribute there are many tied distances. The 5% duplicates figure (p. 11) is a separate dataset fact, not given as a cause of the jumps.

errors.quote: The authors could not reimplement Gan and Tao's method because efficient BCP details are missing
errors.paper: p. 17 only says re-implementation 'is difficult' because crucial details on implementing the BCP subroutine efficiently are missing. It does not say the authors were unable to reimplement it.

best.why: A has no errors and covers all ten points. It adds the Farm/PAMAP2 outcome verdicts, the OPTICS-plot readings and a careful scope critique, so it is slightly more complete than B and avoids C's small overstatements.
